data.title: Pennsylvania reports teen as fourth measles death amid feud with RFK Jr.
data.description:
Pennsylvania officials on Tuesday reported two additional measles-related deaths, bringing the total for the year to four. 

This is a record-setting year for measles in the U.S. The number of cases is at a 35-year high and there are more deaths than any year since 1992. 

The newest death according to state health officials was an unvaccinated person who lived in Mifflin County, located in Central Pennsylvania. County coroner Andrea L. Alcalde in a news release said an 18-year-old died from acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a “rare and severe neurological complication of measles.” 

The coroner did not release any other details, including when the person died.

The state health department also confirmed a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County died from measles complications. County officials first reported the death over the weekend. 

In late August, state officials announced the state’s first measles-associated deaths in 35 years in Lancaster County. The county coroner later disclosed that it was two infants who died.

One of the deaths he attributed directly to measles, while the other died shortly after birth from a ruptured spleen. The coroner said measles contributed to that death, but was not a direct cause.  

The state said that it has now confirmed 693 cases of measles in 38 counties in this year’s outbreak. Nationally, more than 3,200 measles cases have been reported. 

“My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly-contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said in a statement.  

“We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR vaccine – which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades,” Bogen said. 

The best protection against measles remains getting fully vaccinated, according to the Pennsylvania Health Department as well as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.  

The MMR vaccine, administered over two doses, boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97 percent lifetime protection.    

Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, but cases are surging due to low vaccination rates, and the U.S. is at risk of losing that elimination status.  

“These are tragedies, and four families are grieving,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) wrote Tuesday on X.  

The announcement of the additional deaths comes amid an ongoing bitter political feud between Shapiro, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.  

The feud continued Tuesday, when Shapiro lashed out at Kennedy. 

“This serious situation continues to be made worse by RFK Jr. playing games with public health and safety. It’s long past time for @SecKennedy to stop stoking vaccine skepticism and misinformation and compromising the serious mission of the nation’s public health agencies,” Shapiro wrote. 

Kennedy in turn blamed Shapiro for politicizing the outbreak. 

“He continues to point the finger at me and the federal government and to malign the Amish while refusing the federal assistance that might help end the outbreak,” Kennedy wrote on X.  

“I have offered the Governor CDC Epi-Aid, which would put CDC epidemiologists on the ground to help the state respond. Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin requested Epi-Aids and worked alongside CDC teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control,” Kennedy wrote.  

But states don’t always request epi-aids. For instance, Utah had a recent measles outbreak but Kennedy did not mention whether officials there had asked for assistance.  

Meanwhile, the CDC has been excluding the two Lancaster County deaths from its weekly updates of a national measles death tally, a radical departure from the typical agency practice of accepting a state’s own reporting. 

The decision to exclude the deaths reportedly came from the CDC’s new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, at the behest of Kennedy.

Shapiro on Tuesday called out Kennedy’s role in deciding against counting the deaths.

“It is also deeply concerning to learn that the Secretary personally intervened in an otherwise administrative process to direct the CDC to not report these Pennsylvania deaths, presumably because it doesn’t fit his phony narrative,” Shapiro wrote.

Kennedy denied CDC was trying to suppress the information, and said the agency was merely “applying a consistent national standard rather than allowing politicians to decide which deaths appear in federal mortality statistics.”

data.title: Live results: McBride seeks second term as Delaware's lone House lawmaker
data.description:
Voters in the First State head to the polls on Tuesday for the Democratic and Republican primaries for their lone U.S. House seat.

First-term Rep. Sarah McBride (D-Del.) begins her reelection effort running unopposed in the Democratic primary after taking over the seat from now-Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) in 2025. McBride is the first transgender person to serve in Congress.

Three Republicans are running in the primary to challenge McBride, including her former opponent in the 2024 Democratic primary and Republican nominee she defeated in 2024.

Earl Cooper, who received 16 percent of the vote in that primary to McBride’s 80 percent, is seeking a rematch but running as a Republican. He’ll first have to get past medical doctor Joseph Arminio and retired business owner John J. Whalen, who was the 2024 Republican nominee for the seat against McBride.

Polls close at 8 p.m. EDT. Follow decision Desk HQ below.

data.title: Live results: Coons looks to fend off challenger in Delaware Senate primary
data.description:
Voters in the First State head to the polls on Tuesday to cast their ballots in the Democratic and Republican primaries, closing out the primary season for 2026.

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) has held his Senate seat for 16 years, taking over the seat vacated by Joe Biden when he became vice president in 2009 and briefly held by Ted Kaufman. His path to his third full term begins Tuesday night with the Democratic primary, where his challenge is former business executive Eric Hansen, who will appear on the ballot as “E. No-Trump Hansen” after legally changing his name.

Hansen was the Republican nominee in Delaware’s 2024 Senate race, in which he lost to Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.).

On the Republican side, former Democratic state senator Michael Katz and U.S. Army War College instructor John Shulli are vying to be the GOP standard-bearer in the reliably blue state.

Polls close at 8 p.m. EDT. Follow Decision Desk HQ’s live results below.

data.title: House sinks Al Green bid to impeach Trump
data.description:
House lawmakers voted Tuesday to sink a Democratic effort to impeach President Trump over the administration’s aggressive deportation agenda. 

Sponsored by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas), the resolution accused Trump of abusing his powers by launching an immigration crackdown that led to the killing of several civilians earlier in the year.

The vote was 232-147 to shelve the measure, with eighteen Democrats joining almost every Republican in voting to table the resolution. Forty-seven lawmakers voted “present,” including the top Democratic leaders: Reps. Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Katherine Clark (Mass.) and Pete Aguilar (Calif.). 

Democratic leaders said their noncommittal votes reflected the fact that the impeachment articles were brought to the floor without any formal investigations, hearings or broader examination of the charges they contained. 

“None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda,” the Democratic leaders said Monday night in a joint statement.

But there are other reasons for their cautious approach. 

Democrats are bullish about their chances of flipping control of the House in November’s midterms, and they want to keep a disciplined focus on the volatile economy and high cost of living under Trump’s second term, which they see as the best message for achieving that goal. 

Impeachment, while supported by many liberals, also risks distracting from the broader economic message, which has a better chance of resonating with moderate and independent voters who might want a check on Trump, but don’t support ousting him altogether. 

Some Democrats are also worried that impeaching Trump would only animate the president’s supporters to get to the polls, making it tougher for Democrats to flip the House in the midterms. 

Heading into Tuesday’s vote, Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, further distanced party leaders from the resolution.

“This is something oftentimes I think the right-wing media wants us to talk about,” Aguilar said. “But it’s not anything that’s top of the agenda for House Democrats.”

Green, for his part, has been undeterred. A 22-year House veteran and staunch liberal representing Houston, he says Trump’s actions have left him no choice but to pursue impeachment. A failure to do so, he says, would send the message to future presidents that Trump’s actions did not rise to the level of impeachment. 

“The issue isn’t whether the President is guilty of impeachable offenses, because he is,” Green wrote last week to his House colleagues urging their support. “The super salient issue is: What will the U.S. House of Representatives (which has the sole power to impeach) do about it?”

Green’s impeachment articles focused on the administration’s deportation surge earlier in the year, when members of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) conducted aggressive raids around the country in search of undocumented immigrants.

In the course of those operations, federal enforcement officers killed a handful of civilians, including Renée Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis; Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston; and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. 

The administration has defended the killings, saying federal officers feared for their lives in each instance and were merely acting in self defense — an argument disputed by the victims’ relatives, camera footage or both. 

Green’s impeachment articles named those victims, accusing the president of “operating vicious, quota-driven, unaccountable paramilitary forces killing people.”

“President Trump, using the powers of his high office, individually and in coordination with officers in his administration, has transformed ICE and CBP into dangerous, unaccountable paramilitary police forces that operate without oversight and pose a direct threat to the constitutional order of the United States and the people of the United States,” the articles read.

“By such abuses of power, President Trump is brazenly and wantonly devolving the United States democratic republic into an authoritarian regime.”

Green is no stranger to clashes with Trump. Under the president’s first term, Green was among the first Democrats to pursue impeachment, even when party leaders remained cold to the idea. (They would eventually change their tune, voting twice to impeach Trump during his first term). 

More recently, Green made waves in the Capitol for heckling Trump during his appearances before joint sessions of Congress in both 2025 and 2026. For the earlier incident, House lawmakers voted to censure Green. 

The outbursts have frustrated some Democrats in the Capitol, who want the party to stay focused on kitchen table economics. Those critics need not worry about another round of Green impeachment resolutions next year. In May, the longtime Democrat lost his primary, a victim of the Republicans’ national redistricting campaign.

data.title: Democrats want to investigate Russian influence in Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding
data.description:
A Democratic senator is pressing the Trump administration to look into reports that a Russian oligarch paid for wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr., the son of President Donald Trump. 

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who has traveled frequently to Ukraine amid its war with Russia, brought up the issue during a hearing Tuesday while questioning FBI Director Kash Patel. 

Patel denied that the reports were necessarily accurate and said he did not review them before the hearing Tuesday morning. 

“You’re referring to something that happened yesterday in public reporting, and public reporting generally isn’t accurate,” said Patel, saying the FBI would look at “whatever information comes our way.” 

Blumenthal asked Patel to report back to the Senate Judiciary Committee with steps the FBI was taking to investigate improper influence by Kremlev. 

“I was surprised beyond words,” Blumenthal later told The Hill about the reporting. “I was absolutely astonished and appalled that a Russian oligarch with ties to Vladimir Putin is bankrolling the president’s son’s wedding. It’s beyond belief.”

ProPublica reported Monday that a wealthy Russian businessman named Umar Kremlev, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, paid for and attended lavish wedding celebrations for Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, on a private island in the Bahamas in May. 

Anderson in a post on Instagram said the festivities were not the wedding itself, but confirmed that Kremlev is a “dear friend” who hosted two nights of “celebrations” as a gift. 

Attorney General Todd Blanche, at a White House press briefing on Tuesday, dismissed the idea that an investigation was needed, saying he didn’t know “this person” Kremlev and neither did Trump.

“Am I investigating what? And when you say, this person is a friend of Putin, I don’t even know whether that’s true or not,” Blanche said in response to a reporter’s question. “I think all the relevant people involved, the president and his kids have already addressed it, I don’t have any information, I don’t know this person either.”

Democrats in the House are also clamoring for answers on whether there was compromised intelligence or other unethical exchanges as a result of the friendship between the couple and Kremlev. 

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) told reporters Monday that the Trump family “are in the pocket of everyone but the American people.” 

“I said it two years ago, and I’m saying it again. This administration … they are selling out every single person in this country for a buck, and it’s disgusting. And for what? To have a couple of extra frills at your wedding?”

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, posted on social media in response to the ProPublica story that he wanted more information on any quid pro quo Kremlev might have received from the Trump family. 

“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia wrote. “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.” 

Republicans in Congress were generally not focused on the situation on Monday and Tuesday. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) told The Hill that his constituents are not talking about the Trump wedding. 

“I heard about the thing, and same time we’re talking affordability back home, and we’re talking cattle prices back home,” Rounds said. “His wedding was a pretty low priority.”

data.title: Democrats favored over Republicans on health care, immigration, economy: Survey
data.description:
Democrats are ahead of Republicans on some of the issues most important to voters —immigration, health care and the economy—according to a new poll.

In the New York Times/Siena University poll, 51 percent of likely voter respondents said they trusted Democrats to excel in their work on the economy over Republicans, while 45 percent said the same of Republicans in comparison to Democrats and 4 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

When it came to the topic of immigration, 52 percent of respondents backed Democrats’ performance over Republicans, while 45 percent backed Republicans over Democrats and 3 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

And when it came to health care, 60 percent of respondents backed Democrats’ performance over Republicans, while 36 percent backed Republicans over Democrats and 5 percent were unsure or did not answer the question.

The Times/Siena poll spells trouble for Republicans as the midterms elections are only a few weeks out. The party is already dealing with issues like President Trump’s slumping approval rating, the unpopular war in Iran that is nearing its seventh month and Democrats recently excelling on the generic congressional ballot.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.5 percent as of late Tuesday afternoon, while his disapproval rating was at 58.2 percent.

However, a top political adviser to Trump recently said he was “cautiously optimistic” that Republicans can hold onto Congress.

“I won’t predict, you know, how many seats are going to be in either chamber come November,” James Blair told NBC News’s podcast, “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition.” “But, I do think there is a path for us to retain both majorities and defy history.”

The Times/Siena poll took place between Sept. 8 and 13, featuring 1,503 likely voters and a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.

data.title: Fetterman again says he's 'not going to be a Republican' following RNC convention video appearance
data.description:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Penn.) again emphasized that he would not be switching parties Tuesday following his video appearance at the Republican National Committee (RNC) midterm convention. 

When asked by a reporter at Capitol Hill if there was a chance he would become a Republican, Fetterman appeared to become frustrated.

“I’m not going to be a Republican. Why can’t you guys just wait till the midterms? And if I turn a Republican, then I’ll be a liar,” he said. “My name is not on the ballot. Chill.”

“I’ve always been a Democrat. It’s like, no matter how many times I say that, I’m still getting asked just getting into the elevator,” the lawmaker added.

Democratic colleagues grew frustrated with Fetterman following a video he made introducing his fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick (R) at the GOP midterm convention — describing him as a “great friend.”

The pair have built a close relationship as earlier in the summer they launched a joint political action committee, Common Ground PA, seeking to target donors who support both lawmakers.

Fetterman said in a statement after the video’s release that he would continue to caucus with Democrats, writing last week, “I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party—and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on.”

Despite the criticism from his own party, Fetterman votes with the Democratic caucus 90 percent of the time — something that he mentions when asked about whether he would leave the party — but he has also split from Democrats on high-profile votes.

This includes the Iran war as Fetterman voted against every Senate war powers resolution introduced in the upper chamber.

Fetterman has said previously at the Hill Nation Summit that he would leave the Democratic Party if it turned its back on Israel entirely.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz have already indicated they would welcome Fetterman to the GOP.

data.title: Ohio city council decides to rename Lake Erie to 'Gulf of Cleveland'
data.description:
The Cleveland, Ohio, City Council on Monday voted to rename a portion of Lake Erie as the “Gulf of Cleveland,” taking a jab at President Trump’s executive order declaring that Lake Ontario be called the “Gulf of America.”

The emergency resolution led by Councilmember Kris Harsh passed in a 13-1 vote and was intended to take effect immediately. The resolution is not legally binding.

Harsh’s speech to attendees ahead of the vote referred to Trump’s order to rename Lake Ontario, as well as ordering the Gulf of Mexico be called “the Gulf of America” last year, and his recent suggestion of calling New Mexico “New America” after a viral social media post falsely claimed he signed such an executive order.

The resolution applies to the 2-mile stretch of water from the city shoreline, from its eastern to its western borders. It additionally requires the city clerk to notify Apple and other national mapping companies about this new name.

“President Trump’s orders to assign new names without reference to history, tradition, and other acts of Congress have opened the door for United States officials to rename other geography,” Harsh said. “Thanks to him, this is a man who clearly isn’t afraid to say what no one is thinking.”

Harsh added that Trump’s moves made him “emboldened” to rename Cleveland’s neighboring Great Lake. He held up a map during his speech that showed “Gulf of Cleveland” written over the portion of the lake closest to the city.

Harsh also speculated on any pushback to the renaming before replying to that hypothetical pushback with “Who cares?”

“Listen to me very carefully and jot this down: Words don’t matter,” he added, later mocking Trump’s style of ending Truth Social posts by saying at the end of his own speech: “Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Trump’s orders to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico were quickly integrated into Google’s and Apple’s online maps and visible to users in the U.S. International users saw both names, while Canadian and Mexican users, respectively, saw the commonly used names of both bodies of water on the platforms.

It also prompted MapQuest downloads to soar, as the company left the names of both bodies of water unchanged.

Google’s change applied to the Gulf of Mexico led the U.S.’s southern neighbor to sue the tech giant in May 2025. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had warned months earlier that changing the Gulf’s name violated her country’s sovereignty.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed back on Trump’s order earlier this month, as the move came on the heels of the trade war between the two countries. Ford said the move resembled “something out of ‘Saturday Night Live.'”

The Seneca Nation also called on Trump to reverse the order, stating that it violated the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua, which established the nation’s territorial borders.

data.title: Ms. Rachel calls out Ed Sheeran after Macklemore dropped from tour following Palestine support
data.description:
Children’s YouTuber Ms. Rachel criticized reports that Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his ongoing tour because of the rapper’s pro-Palestinian advocacy.

“Ed Sheeran is making a political statement to his fans when he does a concert to support Ukraine, but considers Palestine too dangerous and political,” Ms. Rachel, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, wrote in a Tuesday Instagram post.

On Monday, Macklemore said that stadium owners — among them Robert Kraft of the New England Patriots — urged the British singer to oust him from the Loop Tour due to past comments about Palestine. The rapper has posted several images of himself donning the Palestinian flag and shared several infographics about Israel’s war in Gaza to social media.

Accurso herself has a history of activism. In April 2025, she put out a statement online responding to criticism she faced over her calls for the protection of Palestinian children. The YouTuber star has also spoken out against Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities, having read books to detainees in New Jersey’s Delaney Hall in June.

“All children have the right to food, water, medical care and education. All children should be protected from violence,” she wrote in her 2025 statement.

Per The Hollywood Reporter, pro-Israel groups went after Macklemore earlier this month after he called for a “free Palestine” during Sheeran’s Sept. 4 MetLife Stadium concert. Pop artist Pink criticized the rapper for his pro-Palestinian comments, allegedly pushing for his removal from the tour.

In his own Instagram post Tuesday, Sheeran said that tour promoters, not himself, chose to cut Macklemore from Loop.

“Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me,” the British singer wrote.

“Imagine being a Palestinian kid and seeing he did a concert for Ukraine but when over 20,000 Palestinian children are killed he’s silent,” Accurso wrote, referencing Sheeran’s March 2022 performance raising funds for Ukraine after Russia’s invasion.

When his opening act says Palestinians should be free and not in a genocide he lets a billionaire kick him off,” the children’s YouTuber continued.

In an Aug. 2022 Instagram post, Ukrainian band Antytila posed alongside Sheeran with the country’s flag, commending the pop star for “standing by Ukraine.”

“Thank you Ed and all the team! You are great people with huge hearts!” the band wrote.

In a post on Instagram, Macklemore said Sheeran “and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour,” alleging the singer had spoken to him about pro-Palestinian messaging “being hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with.”

The rapper wrote, “I told (Sheeran) if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and when I stood.”

The YouTuber echoed Macklemore in her Tuesday post, saying, “Palestinian kids have been so dehumanized that as they continue to be killed people debate about being political. It’s sick.”

This story was updated at 4:12 p.m. on Sept. 15, 2026.

data.title: Iran war likely to drive up inflation next year, CBO says
data.description:
The U.S. war against Iran is likely to drive up inflation early next year and could cost at least $2 billion a month as long as it continues, according to a new report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO).

The CBO estimated in its Tuesday report that the main economic impact of the conflict is made of pressures caused by the disruptions to shipping through the Red Sea and the reduction of natural gas and oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

The reduction in shipments has increased energy prices and because of it, in the first quarter of 2027, inflation is estimated to be 0.5 percentage points higher than what CBO projected in February this year.

“The agency estimates that the higher rates of inflation attributable to the conflict will boost interest rates on Treasury securities. In CBO’s assessment, interest rates on 3-month Treasury bills are nearly 0.2 percentage points higher in 2026 than the agency estimated this past February,” CBO said in the 19-page report. “By the first half of 2027, such rates are less than 0.1 percentage point higher than previously estimated.”

The war against Iran has cost the Pentagon around $38 billion as of Aug. 1 this year, CBO estimated when factoring in replacing expended munitions, flying hours, assets lost in the conflict and increased fuel costs.

The Pentagon told Congress on Aug. 13 that the cost of war has gone up to over $42 billion, The Hill reported on Tuesday.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate during a hearing in July that the estimated cost of the conflict was $37.5 billion.

“Trump’s illegal war with Iran is a one-two punch that’s burning a hole in Americans’ pockets and burning a hole in our munitions supply, hurting our military readiness,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said in a statement. “This war is a betrayal of the American people, and it needs to end.”

The main cost for the Pentagon would be the “large expenditure” of missile defense interceptors, leaving the U.S. with a reduced inventory for “several years,” according to CBO.

The CBO report came a day after a report from the Pentagon’s watchdog said that U.S. diplomatic facilities in four Gulf countries – Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) – suffered around $184 million in estimated damages from Iranian military strikes.

The watchdog said that the U.S. conflict with Iran “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply” regarding advanced weapons systems.

President Trump and Hegseth have repeatedly said that the U.S. has sufficient weapons stockpiles.

“CBO estimates that the cost to replace the munitions expended through August 1, 2026, is $21.7 billion: $7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile defense interceptors, and $1.2 billion for other munitions,” CBO said in the report.
